title: Fundamental Types
description: The built-in types, the four you will actually use, and the printing surprises each one has.

content.value: Every C++ variable states its type. That lets C++ check your code before it runs, and know how much memory each box needs.
Types built into the language are called **fundamental types**: everything else is built from them. Four cover almost everything you will write.

content.caption: `4.50` printed as `4.5`: a `double` stores the number, not how you typed it. And `false` printed as `0`. More on that below.

content.title: Four boxes, four types
content.caption: Each box only accepts its own kind of value.

items.text: `int`: whole numbers, about minus 2 billion to plus 2 billion.
items.sub: Too big a value does not stop C++: it stores a wrong number (**overflow**). `g++` usually warns.
Like the population of the world.

items.text: `double`: numbers with a decimal point, about 15 digits.
`float`: a smaller, older decimal type. The value ends in `f`.

content.caption: `pi` holds 3.14159265 in full, but `cout` shows at most 6 significant digits. Only the printing is shortened.

items.title: int
items.text: If you would never want half of one, use `int`.

items.title: double
items.text: If it can have a fractional part, use `double`. It is C++'s default for decimals.

content.question: Which type should hold the number 8100000000?
content.explain: It is a whole number, but too big for an `int`. A `long long` holds it.

items.sub: Lower case, no quotes. `cout` prints it as `1` or `0` unless you send `boolalpha`.

items.text: `char`: exactly one character in single quotes.
items.sub: `'A'`, `'7'`, `'?'`. For a whole word you need `string`, the next lesson.

content.caption: Booleans drive every decision in Module 4.

items.title: Compiles
items.text: Lower case `true`. One character in single quotes.

items.title: Error
items.text: `True` is the wrong case. Double quotes make text, not a `char`.

content.question: What does this print?
content.code:
bool gameOver = false;
cout << gameOver << endl;

content.real: Containers that come in fixed sizes
content.text: Each type takes a fixed amount of memory, measured in **bytes**. A byte is 8 bits: eight tiny on or off switches.

content.caption: C++ lets you ask because C++ programmers often care. In Module 8 you work with memory directly.

content.question: Which type uses more memory?
content.explain: A `long long` takes 8 bytes, twice an `int`. That is how it fits much bigger numbers.

steps.note: A count of items: a whole number, so `int`.
Money needs decimals, so `double`. It stores 45.5.
In stock or not: a yes or no, so `bool`.
One size letter: `char`, in single quotes.
Ask `cout` to print bools as words from now on.
The double prints without its trailing zero.
Thanks to `boolalpha`, the bool prints as a word.

content.title: One shop item, the right type for each value

content.value: The others, like `long long`, `float` and `short`, are for when size matters. Until you need them, `int` and `double` are the right defaults.

practice.question: Declare one variable of each of the four main types to describe a book: an `int` for pages, a `double` for price, a `bool` for whether you have read it, and a `char` for its shelf letter. Print all four with labels, with the bool shown as a word.
This program compiles, but two of the values print wrong: C++ quietly squeezed them into the wrong type. Run it, spot which, and change the types so each value is stored properly.
Print the result of `0.1 + 0.2` and see how `cout` rounds it. Then print `1.0 / 3.0` as well and count the digits you get.

quiz.question: Which type would you use for the number of students in a class?
options: double, because numbers are usually decimals
int, because it is a whole count
quiz.explain: You would never have half a student, so a whole number type is right. `int` covers counts up to about two billion.

quiz.question: Which type holds a price like 249.99?
quiz.explain: An `int` cannot hold a decimal point, so the fractional part would be lost. `double` is the normal choice for a number with decimals.

quiz.question: What does `bool ready = true; cout << ready << endl;` print?
quiz.explain: `cout` prints a bool as 1 or 0 unless you send it `boolalpha` first. After `cout << boolalpha;` it would print true.

quiz.question: What is the difference between `'A'` and `"A"`?
options: `'A'` is a char (one character) and `"A"` is text.
There is no difference in C++.
`'A'` is text and `"A"` is a char.
quiz.explain: Single quotes make a `char`, which holds exactly one character. Double quotes make text, which can hold any number of characters.

quiz.question: Which type should hold the number 8100000000?
quiz.explain: An `int` only reaches about two billion, so 8.1 billion would overflow. `long long` holds whole numbers far bigger than that.
